[{"content": "2024 Update on New York City Staffing Trends 
Highlights 
•  The City’s full-time staffing level has 
increased by 2,413 employees since the 
beginning of FY 2024 to reach 284,330 as 
of January 2024.  
•  If maintained at current levels, the City’s 
year-end staffing would increase for the first 
time since FY 2020. 
•  Some agencies (such as the Department of 
Environmental Protection and Department 
of Transportation) are still experiencing 
elevated vacancy rates when compared to 
their pre-pandemic norm. 
•  To help speed up hiring, DCAS reports that 
it has reduced the median time from exam 
administration to exam results completion 
for DCAS-administered exams from an 
average of 318 days in FY 2021 to 
219 days in FY 2023 (below the agency’s 
target of 290 days).  
•  The turnaround time for DCAS-
administered exams averaged 169 days in 
the first four months of FY 2024, down from 
a median time of 222 days during the same 
period one year ago. 
•  The number of applications received for all 
DCAS civil service exams has increased, 
from 75,489 in FY 2021, to 119,599 in 
FY 2023. The number of applicants rose 
sharply during the first four months of 
FY 2024. 
•  OSC estimates that the City’s full-time 
staffing level will total between 283,000 to 
285,500 employees by June 30, 2024. 
The COVID-19 pandemic upended certain norms 
for New York City’s workforce, which experienced 
relatively stable employee attrition rates and 
small vacancy rates in the prior decade. Since 
March 2020, the City implemented multiple 
rounds of hiring restrictions as part of its budget 
gap-closing efforts, which reduced the 
replacement of employees leaving City service. 
The City, like other employers, also faced a 
significant surge in employee attrition beginning 
in 2021, which was likely encouraged by private 
sector offers of higher salaries and flexible work 
arrangements. The outcome has been uneven 
declines in staffing by agency and by occupation. 
The decline in staffing, coupled with a rise in 
demand for certain municipal services (such as 
public assistance), has led to short-term staffing 
shortages in some program areas. Since the last 
staffing update provided by the Office of the State 
Comptroller (OSC) in November 2022, employee 
attrition has stabilized and the City has begun to 
fill its vacancies to address the short-term 
shortages, although progress has been uneven.  
Now that some time has passed since the public 
health emergency ended in May of 2023 and the 
City announced it will be easing the general hiring 
freeze implemented in the fall of 2023, OSC is 
reexamining the City’s progress in achieving its 
latest staffing target.  
Current targets have been revised down from the 
City’s pre-pandemic target as part of several 
rounds of cost savings efforts. This analysis 
identifies the agencies, occupations, and program 
areas that have experienced improvement in their 
staffing metrics as well as those which continue 
to face significant challenges.

Post-Pandemic Update 
In FY 2022, there were 48,864 employee 
separations from payroll (see Figure 1), the 
highest in at least a decade, and nearly 
80 percent higher than the 10-year historical 
average through FY 2021 (27,600 separations 
per year). OSC last reported on City staffing 
using data from August 2022, when the City’s full-
time workforce totaled 281,333 employees, a 
decline of 6.4 percent from a year-end record of 
300,446 employees in FY 2020.  
Elevated attrition over the past few years was 
attributed to a tight labor market, leading to 
private sector offers of higher salaries as well as 
flexible work arrangements. Starting in May 2021, 
City employees were directed to return to the 
office, although the number of in-office days were 
limited so that the overall building occupancy rate 
would not exceed 50 percent. Effective in 
September 2021, the occupancy limit was lifted, 
and all City employees were directed to return to 
work five days a week.  
After two years of separations substantially 
outpacing hirings, the replacement rate began to 
normalize in FY 2023. In that year, separations 
slowed to 39,222, a level of attrition that remained 
much higher than the historical average. Hiring 
was also relatively strong for the second straight 
fiscal year, improving the replacement rate, but it 
was not enough to offset employee attrition in the 
aggregate.  
Staffing to rise in FY 2024 but some 
agencies still face high turnover 
Since the publication of our November 2022 
staffing report, the City’s attrition rates have, in 
the aggregate, declined sharply, and have been 
close to pre-pandemic norms since the beginning 
of FY 2024. For the first time since FY 2020, full-
time staffing levels have begun to increase, albeit 
slowly.  
Attrition in the first seven months of FY 2024 
totaled 21,503 employees, compared to 25,966 
employees during the same period one year ago 
(see Figure 2) and 33,429 employees in FY 2022. 
During fiscal years 2016 through 2019, 
separations from payroll averaged 19,230 
employees during the same seven-month period.  
While the City’s overall attrition rates have 
improved substantially since FY 2022, some 
agencies continue to experience employee 
attrition that greatly exceeds their pre-pandemic 
average. Figure 3 shows the 10 agencies 
currently experiencing the highest percent 
increase in attrition when the year-to-date attrition 
at these agencies is compared to their pre-
pandemic average. For example, the Department 
of Probation experienced, on average, 67 
separations from payroll from July through 
January of each year prior to the pandemic.

Highlights 
•  The City’s full-time staffing level has 
increased by 2,413 employees since the 
beginning of FY 2024 to reach 284,330 as 
of January 2024.  
•  If maintained at current levels, the City’s 
year-end staffing would increase for the first 
time since FY 2020. 
•  Some agencies (such as the Department of 
Environmental Protection and Department 
of Transportation) are still experiencing 
elevated vacancy rates when compared to 
their pre-pandemic norm. 
•  To help speed up hiring, DCAS reports that 
it has reduced the median time from exam 
administration to exam results completion 
for DCAS-administered exams from an 
average of 318 days in FY 2021 to 
219 days in FY 2023 (below the agency’s 
target of 290 days).  
•  The turnaround time for DCAS-
administered exams averaged 169 days in 
the first four months of FY 2024, down from 
a median time of 222 days during the same 
period one year ago. 
•  The number of applications received for all 
DCAS civil service exams has increased, 
from 75,489 in FY 2021, to 119,599 in 
FY 2023. The number of applicants rose 
sharply during the first four months of 
FY 2024. 
•  OSC estimates that the City’s full-time 
staffing level will total between 283,000 to 
285,500 employees by June 30, 2024. 
The COVID-19 pandemic upended certain norms 
for New York City’s workforce, which experienced 
relatively stable employee attrition rates and 
small vacancy rates in the prior decade. Since 
March 2020, the City implemented multiple 
rounds of hiring restrictions as part of its budget 
gap-closing efforts, which reduced the 
replacement of employees leaving City service. 
The City, like other employers, also faced a 
significant surge in employee attrition beginning 
in 2021, which was likely encouraged by private 
sector offers of higher salaries and flexible work 
arrangements. The outcome has been uneven 
declines in staffing by agency and by occupation. 
The decline in staffing, coupled with a rise in 
demand for certain municipal services (such as 
public assistance), has led to short-term staffing 
shortages in some program areas. Since the last 
staffing update provided by the Office of the State 
Comptroller (OSC) in November 2022, employee 
attrition has stabilized and the City has begun to 
fill its vacancies to address the short-term 
shortages, although progress has been uneven.  
Now that some time has passed since the public 
health emergency ended in May of 2023 and the 
City announced it will be easing the general hiring 
freeze implemented in the fall of 2023, OSC is 
reexamining the City’s progress in achieving its 
latest staffing target.  
Current targets have been revised down from the 
City’s pre-pandemic target as part of several 
rounds of cost savings efforts. This analysis 
identifies the agencies, occupations, and program 
areas that have experienced improvement in their 
staffing metrics as well as those which continue 
to face significant challenges.

Post-Pandemic Update 
In FY 2022, there were 48,864 employee 
separations from payroll (see Figure 1), the 
highest in at least a decade, and nearly 
80 percent higher than the 10-year historical 
average through FY 2021 (27,600 separations 
per year). OSC last reported on City staffing 
using data from August 2022, when the City’s full-
time workforce totaled 281,333 employees, a 
decline of 6.4 percent from a year-end record of 
300,446 employees in FY 2020.  
Elevated attrition over the past few years was 
attributed to a tight labor market, leading to 
private sector offers of higher salaries as well as 
flexible work arrangements. Starting in May 2021, 
City employees were directed to return to the 
office, although the number of in-office days were 
limited so that the overall building occupancy rate 
would not exceed 50 percent. Effective in 
September 2021, the occupancy limit was lifted, 
and all City employees were directed to return to 
work five days a week.  
After two years of separations substantially 
outpacing hirings, the replacement rate began to 
normalize in FY 2023. In that year, separations 
slowed to 39,222, a level of attrition that remained 
much higher than the historical average. Hiring 
was also relatively strong for the second straight 
fiscal year, improving the replacement rate, but it 
was not enough to offset employee attrition in the 
aggregate.  
Staffing to rise in FY 2024 but some 
agencies still face high turnover 
Since the publication of our November 2022 
staffing report, the City’s attrition rates have, in 
the aggregate, declined sharply, and have been 
close to pre-pandemic norms since the beginning 
of FY 2024. For the first time since FY 2020, full-
time staffing levels have begun to increase, albeit 
slowly.  
Attrition in the first seven months of FY 2024 
totaled 21,503 employees, compared to 25,966 
employees during the same period one year ago 
(see Figure 2) and 33,429 employees in FY 2022. 
During fiscal years 2016 through 2019, 
separations from payroll averaged 19,230 
employees during the same seven-month period.  
While the City’s overall attrition rates have 
improved substantially since FY 2022, some 
agencies continue to experience employee 
attrition that greatly exceeds their pre-pandemic 
average. Figure 3 shows the 10 agencies 
currently experiencing the highest percent 
increase in attrition when the year-to-date attrition 
at these agencies is compared to their pre-
pandemic average. For example, the Department 
of Probation experienced, on average, 67 
separations from payroll from July through 
January of each year prior to the pandemic.

[{"content": "2024 Update on New York City Staffing Trends 
Highlights 
•  The City’s full-time staffing level has 
increased by 2,413 employees since the 
beginning of FY 2024 to reach 284,330 as 
of January 2024.  
•  If maintained at current levels, the City’s 
year-end staffing would increase for the first 
time since FY 2020. 
•  Some agencies (such as the Department of 
Environmental Protection and Department 
of Transportation) are still experiencing 
elevated vacancy rates when compared to 
their pre-pandemic norm. 
•  To help speed up hiring, DCAS reports that 
it has reduced the median time from exam 
administration to exam results completion 
for DCAS-administered exams from an 
average of 318 days in FY 2021 to 
219 days in FY 2023 (below the agency’s 
target of 290 days).  
•  The turnaround time for DCAS-
administered exams averaged 169 days in 
the first four months of FY 2024, down from 
a median time of 222 days during the same 
period one year ago. 
•  The number of applications received for all 
DCAS civil service exams has increased, 
from 75,489 in FY 2021, to 119,599 in 
FY 2023. The number of applicants rose 
sharply during the first four months of 
FY 2024. 
•  OSC estimates that the City’s full-time 
staffing level will total between 283,000 to 
285,500 employees by June 30, 2024. 
The COVID-19 pandemic upended certain norms 
for New York City’s workforce, which experienced 
relatively stable employee attrition rates and 
small vacancy rates in the prior decade. Since 
March 2020, the City implemented multiple 
rounds of hiring restrictions as part of its budget 
gap-closing efforts, which reduced the 
replacement of employees leaving City service. 
The City, like other employers, also faced a 
significant surge in employee attrition beginning 
in 2021, which was likely encouraged by private 
sector offers of higher salaries and flexible work 
arrangements. The outcome has been uneven 
declines in staffing by agency and by occupation. 
The decline in staffing, coupled with a rise in 
demand for certain municipal services (such as 
public assistance), has led to short-term staffing 
shortages in some program areas. Since the last 
staffing update provided by the Office of the State 
Comptroller (OSC) in November 2022, employee 
attrition has stabilized and the City has begun to 
fill its vacancies to address the short-term 
shortages, although progress has been uneven.  
Now that some time has passed since the public 
health emergency ended in May of 2023 and the 
City announced it will be easing the general hiring 
freeze implemented in the fall of 2023, OSC is 
reexamining the City’s progress in achieving its 
latest staffing target.  
Current targets have been revised down from the 
City’s pre-pandemic target as part of several 
rounds of cost savings efforts. This analysis 
identifies the agencies, occupations, and program 
areas that have experienced improvement in their 
staffing metrics as well as those which continue 
to face significant challenges.

Post-Pandemic Update 
In FY 2022, there were 48,864 employee 
separations from payroll (see Figure 1), the 
highest in at least a decade, and nearly 
80 percent higher than the 10-year historical 
average through FY 2021 (27,600 separations 
per year). OSC last reported on City staffing 
using data from August 2022, when the City’s full-
time workforce totaled 281,333 employees, a 
decline of 6.4 percent from a year-end record of 
300,446 employees in FY 2020.  
Elevated attrition over the past few years was 
attributed to a tight labor market, leading to 
private sector offers of higher salaries as well as 
flexible work arrangements. Starting in May 2021, 
City employees were directed to return to the 
office, although the number of in-office days were 
limited so that the overall building occupancy rate 
would not exceed 50 percent. Effective in 
September 2021, the occupancy limit was lifted, 
and all City employees were directed to return to 
work five days a week.  
After two years of separations substantially 
outpacing hirings, the replacement rate began to 
normalize in FY 2023. In that year, separations 
slowed to 39,222, a level of attrition that remained 
much higher than the historical average. Hiring 
was also relatively strong for the second straight 
fiscal year, improving the replacement rate, but it 
was not enough to offset employee attrition in the 
aggregate.  
Staffing to rise in FY 2024 but some 
agencies still face high turnover 
Since the publication of our November 2022 
staffing report, the City’s attrition rates have, in 
the aggregate, declined sharply, and have been 
close to pre-pandemic norms since the beginning 
of FY 2024. For the first time since FY 2020, full-
time staffing levels have begun to increase, albeit 
slowly.  
Attrition in the first seven months of FY 2024 
totaled 21,503 employees, compared to 25,966 
employees during the same period one year ago 
(see Figure 2) and 33,429 employees in FY 2022. 
During fiscal years 2016 through 2019, 
separations from payroll averaged 19,230 
employees during the same seven-month period.  
While the City’s overall attrition rates have 
improved substantially since FY 2022, some 
agencies continue to experience employee 
attrition that greatly exceeds their pre-pandemic 
average. Figure 3 shows the 10 agencies 
currently experiencing the highest percent 
increase in attrition when the year-to-date attrition 
at these agencies is compared to their pre-
pandemic average. For example, the Department 
of Probation experienced, on average, 67 
separations from payroll from July through 
January of each year prior to the pandemic.

Highlights 
•  The City’s full-time staffing level has 
increased by 2,413 employees since the 
beginning of FY 2024 to reach 284,330 as 
of January 2024.  
•  If maintained at current levels, the City’s 
year-end staffing would increase for the first 
time since FY 2020. 
•  Some agencies (such as the Department of 
Environmental Protection and Department 
of Transportation) are still experiencing 
elevated vacancy rates when compared to 
their pre-pandemic norm. 
•  To help speed up hiring, DCAS reports that 
it has reduced the median time from exam 
administration to exam results completion 
for DCAS-administered exams from an 
average of 318 days in FY 2021 to 
219 days in FY 2023 (below the agency’s 
target of 290 days).  
•  The turnaround time for DCAS-
administered exams averaged 169 days in 
the first four months of FY 2024, down from 
a median time of 222 days during the same 
period one year ago. 
•  The number of applications received for all 
DCAS civil service exams has increased, 
from 75,489 in FY 2021, to 119,599 in 
FY 2023. The number of applicants rose 
sharply during the first four months of 
FY 2024. 
•  OSC estimates that the City’s full-time 
staffing level will total between 283,000 to 
285,500 employees by June 30, 2024. 
The COVID-19 pandemic upended certain norms 
for New York City’s workforce, which experienced 
relatively stable employee attrition rates and 
small vacancy rates in the prior decade. Since 
March 2020, the City implemented multiple 
rounds of hiring restrictions as part of its budget 
gap-closing efforts, which reduced the 
replacement of employees leaving City service. 
The City, like other employers, also faced a 
significant surge in employee attrition beginning 
in 2021, which was likely encouraged by private 
sector offers of higher salaries and flexible work 
arrangements. The outcome has been uneven 
declines in staffing by agency and by occupation. 
The decline in staffing, coupled with a rise in 
demand for certain municipal services (such as 
public assistance), has led to short-term staffing 
shortages in some program areas. Since the last 
staffing update provided by the Office of the State 
Comptroller (OSC) in November 2022, employee 
attrition has stabilized and the City has begun to 
fill its vacancies to address the short-term 
shortages, although progress has been uneven.  
Now that some time has passed since the public 
health emergency ended in May of 2023 and the 
City announced it will be easing the general hiring 
freeze implemented in the fall of 2023, OSC is 
reexamining the City’s progress in achieving its 
latest staffing target.  
Current targets have been revised down from the 
City’s pre-pandemic target as part of several 
rounds of cost savings efforts. This analysis 
identifies the agencies, occupations, and program 
areas that have experienced improvement in their 
staffing metrics as well as those which continue 
to face significant challenges.

Post-Pandemic Update 
In FY 2022, there were 48,864 employee 
separations from payroll (see Figure 1), the 
highest in at least a decade, and nearly 
80 percent higher than the 10-year historical 
average through FY 2021 (27,600 separations 
per year). OSC last reported on City staffing 
using data from August 2022, when the City’s full-
time workforce totaled 281,333 employees, a 
decline of 6.4 percent from a year-end record of 
300,446 employees in FY 2020.  
Elevated attrition over the past few years was 
attributed to a tight labor market, leading to 
private sector offers of higher salaries as well as 
flexible work arrangements. Starting in May 2021, 
City employees were directed to return to the 
office, although the number of in-office days were 
limited so that the overall building occupancy rate 
would not exceed 50 percent. Effective in 
September 2021, the occupancy limit was lifted, 
and all City employees were directed to return to 
work five days a week.  
After two years of separations substantially 
outpacing hirings, the replacement rate began to 
normalize in FY 2023. In that year, separations 
slowed to 39,222, a level of attrition that remained 
much higher than the historical average. Hiring 
was also relatively strong for the second straight 
fiscal year, improving the replacement rate, but it 
was not enough to offset employee attrition in the 
aggregate.  
Staffing to rise in FY 2024 but some 
agencies still face high turnover 
Since the publication of our November 2022 
staffing report, the City’s attrition rates have, in 
the aggregate, declined sharply, and have been 
close to pre-pandemic norms since the beginning 
of FY 2024. For the first time since FY 2020, full-
time staffing levels have begun to increase, albeit 
slowly.  
Attrition in the first seven months of FY 2024 
totaled 21,503 employees, compared to 25,966 
employees during the same period one year ago 
(see Figure 2) and 33,429 employees in FY 2022. 
During fiscal years 2016 through 2019, 
separations from payroll averaged 19,230 
employees during the same seven-month period.  
While the City’s overall attrition rates have 
improved substantially since FY 2022, some 
agencies continue to experience employee 
attrition that greatly exceeds their pre-pandemic 
average. Figure 3 shows the 10 agencies 
currently experiencing the highest percent 
increase in attrition when the year-to-date attrition 
at these agencies is compared to their pre-
pandemic average. For example, the Department 
of Probation experienced, on average, 67 
separations from payroll from July through 
January of each year prior to the pandemic.

[{"content": "2024 Update on New York City Staffing Trends 
Highlights 
•  The City’s full-time staffing level has 
increased by 2,413 employees since the 
beginning of FY 2024 to reach 284,330 as 
of January 2024.  
•  If maintained at current levels, the City’s 
year-end staffing would increase for the first 
time since FY 2020. 
•  Some agencies (such as the Department of 
Environmental Protection and Department 
of Transportation) are still experiencing 
elevated vacancy rates when compared to 
their pre-pandemic norm. 
•  To help speed up hiring, DCAS reports that 
it has reduced the median time from exam 
administration to exam results completion 
for DCAS-administered exams from an 
average of 318 days in FY 2021 to 
219 days in FY 2023 (below the agency’s 
target of 290 days).  
•  The turnaround time for DCAS-
administered exams averaged 169 days in 
the first four months of FY 2024, down from 
a median time of 222 days during the same 
period one year ago. 
•  The number of applications received for all 
DCAS civil service exams has increased, 
from 75,489 in FY 2021, to 119,599 in 
FY 2023. The number of applicants rose 
sharply during the first four months of 
FY 2024. 
•  OSC estimates that the City’s full-time 
staffing level will total between 283,000 to 
285,500 employees by June 30, 2024. 
The COVID-19 pandemic upended certain norms 
for New York City’s workforce, which experienced 
relatively stable employee attrition rates and 
small vacancy rates in the prior decade. Since 
March 2020, the City implemented multiple 
rounds of hiring restrictions as part of its budget 
gap-closing efforts, which reduced the 
replacement of employees leaving City service. 
The City, like other employers, also faced a 
significant surge in employee attrition beginning 
in 2021, which was likely encouraged by private 
sector offers of higher salaries and flexible work 
arrangements. The outcome has been uneven 
declines in staffing by agency and by occupation. 
The decline in staffing, coupled with a rise in 
demand for certain municipal services (such as 
public assistance), has led to short-term staffing 
shortages in some program areas. Since the last 
staffing update provided by the Office of the State 
Comptroller (OSC) in November 2022, employee 
attrition has stabilized and the City has begun to 
fill its vacancies to address the short-term 
shortages, although progress has been uneven.  
Now that some time has passed since the public 
health emergency ended in May of 2023 and the 
City announced it will be easing the general hiring 
freeze implemented in the fall of 2023, OSC is 
reexamining the City’s progress in achieving its 
latest staffing target.  
Current targets have been revised down from the 
City’s pre-pandemic target as part of several 
rounds of cost savings efforts. This analysis 
identifies the agencies, occupations, and program 
areas that have experienced improvement in their 
staffing metrics as well as those which continue 
to face significant challenges.

Highlights 
•  The City’s full-time staffing level has 
increased by 2,413 employees since the 
beginning of FY 2024 to reach 284,330 as 
of January 2024.  
•  If maintained at current levels, the City’s 
year-end staffing would increase for the first 
time since FY 2020. 
•  Some agencies (such as the Department of 
Environmental Protection and Department 
of Transportation) are still experiencing 
elevated vacancy rates when compared to 
their pre-pandemic norm. 
•  To help speed up hiring, DCAS reports that 
it has reduced the median time from exam 
administration to exam results completion 
for DCAS-administered exams from an 
average of 318 days in FY 2021 to 
219 days in FY 2023 (below the agency’s 
target of 290 days).  
•  The turnaround time for DCAS-
administered exams averaged 169 days in 
the first four months of FY 2024, down from 
a median time of 222 days during the same 
period one year ago. 
•  The number of applications received for all 
DCAS civil service exams has increased, 
from 75,489 in FY 2021, to 119,599 in 
FY 2023. The number of applicants rose 
sharply during the first four months of 
FY 2024. 
•  OSC estimates that the City’s full-time 
staffing level will total between 283,000 to 
285,500 employees by June 30, 2024. 
The COVID-19 pandemic upended certain norms 
for New York City’s workforce, which experienced 
relatively stable employee attrition rates and 
small vacancy rates in the prior decade. Since 
March 2020, the City implemented multiple 
rounds of hiring restrictions as part of its budget 
gap-closing efforts, which reduced the 
replacement of employees leaving City service. 
The City, like other employers, also faced a 
significant surge in employee attrition beginning 
in 2021, which was likely encouraged by private 
sector offers of higher salaries and flexible work 
arrangements. The outcome has been uneven 
declines in staffing by agency and by occupation. 
The decline in staffing, coupled with a rise in 
demand for certain municipal services (such as 
public assistance), has led to short-term staffing 
shortages in some program areas. Since the last 
staffing update provided by the Office of the State 
Comptroller (OSC) in November 2022, employee 
attrition has stabilized and the City has begun to 
fill its vacancies to address the short-term 
shortages, although progress has been uneven.  
Now that some time has passed since the public 
health emergency ended in May of 2023 and the 
City announced it will be easing the general hiring 
freeze implemented in the fall of 2023, OSC is 
reexamining the City’s progress in achieving its 
latest staffing target.  
Current targets have been revised down from the 
City’s pre-pandemic target as part of several 
rounds of cost savings efforts. This analysis 
identifies the agencies, occupations, and program 
areas that have experienced improvement in their 
staffing metrics as well as those which continue 
to face significant challenges.

Fiscal Year
Post-Pandemic Update 
In FY 2022, there were 48,864 employee 
separations from payroll (see Figure 1), the 
highest in at least a decade, and nearly 
80 percent higher than the 10-year historical 
average through FY 2021 (27,600 separations 
per year). OSC last reported on City staffing 
using data from August 2022, when the City’s full-
time workforce totaled 281,333 employees, a 
decline of 6.4 percent from a year-end record of 
300,446 employees in FY 2020.  
Elevated attrition over the past few years was 
attributed to a tight labor market, leading to 
private sector offers of higher salaries as well as 
flexible work arrangements. Starting in May 2021, 
City employees were directed to return to the 
office, although the number of in-office days were 
limited so that the overall building occupancy rate 
would not exceed 50 percent. Effective in 
September 2021, the occupancy limit was lifted, 
and all City employees were directed to return to 
work five days a week.  
After two years of separations substantially 
outpacing hirings, the replacement rate began to 
normalize in FY 2023. In that year, separations 
slowed to 39,222, a level of attrition that remained 
much higher than the historical average. Hiring 
was also relatively strong for the second straight 
fiscal year, improving the replacement rate, but it 
was not enough to offset employee attrition in the 
aggregate.  
Staffing to rise in FY 2024 but some 
agencies still face high turnover 
Since the publication of our November 2022 
staffing report, the City’s attrition rates have, in 
the aggregate, declined sharply, and have been 
close to pre-pandemic norms since the beginning 
of FY 2024. For the first time since FY 2020, full-
time staffing levels have begun to increase, albeit 
slowly.  
Attrition in the first seven months of FY 2024 
totaled 21,503 employees, compared to 25,966 
employees during the same period one year ago 
(see Figure 2) and 33,429 employees in FY 2022. 
During fiscal years 2016 through 2019, 
separations from payroll averaged 19,230 
employees during the same seven-month period.  
While the City’s overall attrition rates have 
improved substantially since FY 2022, some 
agencies continue to experience employee 
attrition that greatly exceeds their pre-pandemic 
average. Figure 3 shows the 10 agencies 
currently experiencing the highest percent 
increase in attrition when the year-to-date attrition 
at these agencies is compared to their pre-
pandemic average. For example, the Department 
of Probation experienced, on average, 67 
separations from payroll from July through 
January of each year prior to the pandemic.

[{"content": "2024 Update on New York City Staffing Trends 
Highlights 
•  The City’s full-time staffing level has 
increased by 2,413 employees since the 
beginning of FY 2024 to reach 284,330 as 
of January 2024.  
•  If maintained at current levels, the City’s 
year-end staffing would increase for the first 
time since FY 2020. 
•  Some agencies (such as the Department of 
Environmental Protection and Department 
of Transportation) are still experiencing 
elevated vacancy rates when compared to 
their pre-pandemic norm. 
•  To help speed up hiring, DCAS reports that 
it has reduced the median time from exam 
administration to exam results completion 
for DCAS-administered exams from an 
average of 318 days in FY 2021 to 
219 days in FY 2023 (below the agency’s 
target of 290 days).  
•  The turnaround time for DCAS-
administered exams averaged 169 days in 
the first four months of FY 2024, down from 
a median time of 222 days during the same 
period one year ago. 
•  The number of applications received for all 
DCAS civil service exams has increased, 
from 75,489 in FY 2021, to 119,599 in 
FY 2023. The number of applicants rose 
sharply during the first four months of 
FY 2024. 
•  OSC estimates that the City’s full-time 
staffing level will total between 283,000 to 
285,500 employees by June 30, 2024. 
The COVID-19 pandemic upended certain norms 
for New York City’s workforce, which experienced 
relatively stable employee attrition rates and 
small vacancy rates in the prior decade. Since 
March 2020, the City implemented multiple 
rounds of hiring restrictions as part of its budget 
gap-closing efforts, which reduced the 
replacement of employees leaving City service. 
The City, like other employers, also faced a 
significant surge in employee attrition beginning 
in 2021, which was likely encouraged by private 
sector offers of higher salaries and flexible work 
arrangements. The outcome has been uneven 
declines in staffing by agency and by occupation. 
The decline in staffing, coupled with a rise in 
demand for certain municipal services (such as 
public assistance), has led to short-term staffing 
shortages in some program areas. Since the last 
staffing update provided by the Office of the State 
Comptroller (OSC) in November 2022, employee 
attrition has stabilized and the City has begun to 
fill its vacancies to address the short-term 
shortages, although progress has been uneven.  
Now that some time has passed since the public 
health emergency ended in May of 2023 and the 
City announced it will be easing the general hiring 
freeze implemented in the fall of 2023, OSC is 
reexamining the City’s progress in achieving its 
latest staffing target.  
Current targets have been revised down from the 
City’s pre-pandemic target as part of several 
rounds of cost savings efforts. This analysis 
identifies the agencies, occupations, and program 
areas that have experienced improvement in their 
staffing metrics as well as those which continue 
to face significant challenges.

Post-Pandemic Update 
In FY 2022, there were 48,864 employee 
separations from payroll (see Figure 1), the 
highest in at least a decade, and nearly 
80 percent higher than the 10-year historical 
average through FY 2021 (27,600 separations 
per year). OSC last reported on City staffing 
using data from August 2022, when the City’s full-
time workforce totaled 281,333 employees, a 
decline of 6.4 percent from a year-end record of 
300,446 employees in FY 2020.  
Elevated attrition over the past few years was 
attributed to a tight labor market, leading to 
private sector offers of higher salaries as well as 
flexible work arrangements. Starting in May 2021, 
City employees were directed to return to the 
office, although the number of in-office days were 
limited so that the overall building occupancy rate 
would not exceed 50 percent. Effective in 
September 2021, the occupancy limit was lifted, 
and all City employees were directed to return to 
work five days a week.  
After two years of separations substantially 
outpacing hirings, the replacement rate began to 
normalize in FY 2023. In that year, separations 
slowed to 39,222, a level of attrition that remained 
much higher than the historical average. Hiring 
was also relatively strong for the second straight 
fiscal year, improving the replacement rate, but it 
was not enough to offset employee attrition in the 
aggregate.  
Staffing to rise in FY 2024 but some 
agencies still face high turnover 
Since the publication of our November 2022 
staffing report, the City’s attrition rates have, in 
the aggregate, declined sharply, and have been 
close to pre-pandemic norms since the beginning 
of FY 2024. For the first time since FY 2020, full-
time staffing levels have begun to increase, albeit 
slowly.  
Attrition in the first seven months of FY 2024 
totaled 21,503 employees, compared to 25,966 
employees during the same period one year ago 
(see Figure 2) and 33,429 employees in FY 2022. 
During fiscal years 2016 through 2019, 
separations from payroll averaged 19,230 
employees during the same seven-month period.

improved substantially since FY 2022, some 
agencies continue to experience employee 
attrition that greatly exceeds their pre-pandemic 
average. Figure 3 shows the 10 agencies 
currently experiencing the highest percent 
increase in attrition when the year-to-date attrition 
at these agencies is compared to their pre-
pandemic average. For example, the Department 
of Probation experienced, on average, 67 
separations from payroll from July through 
January of each year prior to the pandemic.

Highlights 
•  The City’s full-time staffing level has 
increased by 2,413 employees since the 
beginning of FY 2024 to reach 284,330 as 
of January 2024.  
•  If maintained at current levels, the City’s 
year-end staffing would increase for the first 
time since FY 2020. 
•  Some agencies (such as the Department of 
Environmental Protection and Department 
of Transportation) are still experiencing 
elevated vacancy rates when compared to 
their pre-pandemic norm. 
•  To help speed up hiring, DCAS reports that 
it has reduced the median time from exam 
administration to exam results completion 
for DCAS-administered exams from an 
average of 318 days in FY 2021 to 
219 days in FY 2023 (below the agency’s 
target of 290 days).  
•  The turnaround time for DCAS-
administered exams averaged 169 days in 
the first four months of FY 2024, down from 
a median time of 222 days during the same 
period one year ago. 
•  The number of applications received for all 
DCAS civil service exams has increased, 
from 75,489 in FY 2021, to 119,599 in 
FY 2023. The number of applicants rose 
sharply during the first four months of 
FY 2024. 
•  OSC estimates that the City’s full-time 
staffing level will total between 283,000 to 
285,500 employees by June 30, 2024. 
The COVID-19 pandemic upended certain norms 
for New York City’s workforce, which experienced 
relatively stable employee attrition rates and 
small vacancy rates in the prior decade. Since 
March 2020, the City implemented multiple 
rounds of hiring restrictions as part of its budget 
gap-closing efforts, which reduced the 
replacement of employees leaving City service. 
The City, like other employers, also faced a 
significant surge in employee attrition beginning 
in 2021, which was likely encouraged by private 
sector offers of higher salaries and flexible work 
arrangements. The outcome has been uneven 
declines in staffing by agency and by occupation. 
The decline in staffing, coupled with a rise in 
demand for certain municipal services (such as 
public assistance), has led to short-term staffing 
shortages in some program areas. Since the last 
staffing update provided by the Office of the State 
Comptroller (OSC) in November 2022, employee 
attrition has stabilized and the City has begun to 
fill its vacancies to address the short-term 
shortages, although progress has been uneven.  
Now that some time has passed since the public 
health emergency ended in May of 2023 and the 
City announced it will be easing the general hiring 
freeze implemented in the fall of 2023, OSC is 
reexamining the City’s progress in achieving its 
latest staffing target.  
Current targets have been revised down from the 
City’s pre-pandemic target as part of several 
rounds of cost savings efforts. This analysis 
identifies the agencies, occupations, and program 
areas that have experienced improvement in their 
staffing metrics as well as those which continue 
to face significant challenges.

Post-Pandemic Update 
In FY 2022, there were 48,864 employee 
separations from payroll (see Figure 1), the 
highest in at least a decade, and nearly 
80 percent higher than the 10-year historical 
average through FY 2021 (27,600 separations 
per year). OSC last reported on City staffing 
using data from August 2022, when the City’s full-
time workforce totaled 281,333 employees, a 
decline of 6.4 percent from a year-end record of 
300,446 employees in FY 2020.  
Elevated attrition over the past few years was 
attributed to a tight labor market, leading to 
private sector offers of higher salaries as well as 
flexible work arrangements. Starting in May 2021, 
City employees were directed to return to the 
office, although the number of in-office days were 
limited so that the overall building occupancy rate 
would not exceed 50 percent. Effective in 
September 2021, the occupancy limit was lifted, 
and all City employees were directed to return to 
work five days a week.  
After two years of separations substantially 
outpacing hirings, the replacement rate began to 
normalize in FY 2023. In that year, separations 
slowed to 39,222, a level of attrition that remained 
much higher than the historical average. Hiring 
was also relatively strong for the second straight 
fiscal year, improving the replacement rate, but it 
was not enough to offset employee attrition in the 
aggregate.  
Staffing to rise in FY 2024 but some 
agencies still face high turnover 
Since the publication of our November 2022 
staffing report, the City’s attrition rates have, in 
the aggregate, declined sharply, and have been 
close to pre-pandemic norms since the beginning 
of FY 2024. For the first time since FY 2020, full-
time staffing levels have begun to increase, albeit 
slowly.  
Attrition in the first seven months of FY 2024 
totaled 21,503 employees, compared to 25,966 
employees during the same period one year ago 
(see Figure 2) and 33,429 employees in FY 2022. 
During fiscal years 2016 through 2019, 
separations from payroll averaged 19,230 
employees during the same seven-month period.  
While the City’s overall attrition rates have 
improved substantially since FY 2022, some 
agencies continue to experience employee 
attrition that greatly exceeds their pre-pandemic 
average. Figure 3 shows the 10 agencies 
currently experiencing the highest percent 
increase in attrition when the year-to-date attrition 
at these agencies is compared to their pre-
pandemic average. For example, the Department 
of Probation experienced, on average, 67 
separations from payroll from July through 
January of each year prior to the pandemic.

2024 Update on New York City Staffing Trends 
Highlights 
•  The City’s full-time staffing level has 
increased by 2,413 employees since the 
beginning of FY 2024 to reach 284,330 as 
of January 2024.  
•  If maintained at current levels, the City’s 
year-end staffing would increase for the first 
time since FY 2020. 
•  Some agencies (such as the Department of 
Environmental Protection and Department 
of Transportation) are still experiencing 
elevated vacancy rates when compared to 
their pre-pandemic norm. 
•  To help speed up hiring, DCAS reports that 
it has reduced the median time from exam 
administration to exam results completion 
for DCAS-administered exams from an 
average of 318 days in FY 2021 to 
219 days in FY 2023 (below the agency’s 
target of 290 days).  
•  The turnaround time for DCAS-
administered exams averaged 169 days in 
the first four months of FY 2024, down from 
a median time of 222 days during the same 
period one year ago. 
•  The number of applications received for all 
DCAS civil service exams has increased, 
from 75,489 in FY 2021, to 119,599 in 
FY 2023. The number of applicants rose 
sharply during the first four months of 
FY 2024. 
•  OSC estimates that the City’s full-time 
staffing level will total between 283,000 to 
285,500 employees by June 30, 2024. 
The COVID-19 pandemic upended certain norms 
for New York City’s workforce, which experienced 
relatively stable employee attrition rates and 
small vacancy rates in the prior decade. Since 
March 2020, the City implemented multiple 
rounds of hiring restrictions as part of its budget 
gap-closing efforts, which reduced the 
replacement of employees leaving City service. 
The City, like other employers, also faced a 
significant surge in employee attrition beginning 
in 2021, which was likely encouraged by private 
sector offers of higher salaries and flexible work 
arrangements. The outcome has been uneven 
declines in staffing by agency and by occupation. 
The decline in staffing, coupled with a rise in 
demand for certain municipal services (such as 
public assistance), has led to short-term staffing 
shortages in some program areas. Since the last 
staffing update provided by the Office of the State 
Comptroller (OSC) in November 2022, employee 
attrition has stabilized and the City has begun to 
fill its vacancies to address the short-term 
shortages, although progress has been uneven.  
Now that some time has passed since the public 
health emergency ended in May of 2023 and the 
City announced it will be easing the general hiring 
freeze implemented in the fall of 2023, OSC is 
reexamining the City’s progress in achieving its 
latest staffing target.  
Current targets have been revised down from the 
City’s pre-pandemic target as part of several 
rounds of cost savings efforts. This analysis 
identifies the agencies, occupations, and program 
areas that have experienced improvement in their 
staffing metrics as well as those which continue 
to face significant challenges.  
Report 2-2025  |   May 2024

Sources: NYC Office of Management and Budget; OSC analysis
Fiscal Year
Post-Pandemic Update 
In FY 2022, there were 48,864 employee 
separations from payroll (see Figure 1), the 
highest in at least a decade, and nearly 
80 percent higher than the 10-year historical 
average through FY 2021 (27,600 separations 
per year). OSC last reported on City staffing 
using data from August 2022, when the City’s full-
time workforce totaled 281,333 employees, a 
decline of 6.4 percent from a year-end record of 
300,446 employees in FY 2020.  
Elevated attrition over the past few years was 
attributed to a tight labor market, leading to 
private sector offers of higher salaries as well as 
flexible work arrangements. Starting in May 2021, 
City employees were directed to return to the 
office, although the number of in-office days were 
limited so that the overall building occupancy rate 
would not exceed 50 percent. Effective in 
September 2021, the occupancy limit was lifted, 
and all City employees were directed to return to 
work five days a week.  
After two years of separations substantially 
outpacing hirings, the replacement rate began to 
normalize in FY 2023. In that year, separations 
slowed to 39,222, a level of attrition that remained 
much higher than the historical average. Hiring 
was also relatively strong for the second straight 
fiscal year, improving the replacement rate, but it 
was not enough to offset employee attrition in the 
aggregate.  
Staffing to rise in FY 2024 but some 
agencies still face high turnover 
Since the publication of our November 2022 
staffing report, the City’s attrition rates have, in 
the aggregate, declined sharply, and have been 
close to pre-pandemic norms since the beginning 
of FY 2024. For the first time since FY 2020, full-
time staffing levels have begun to increase, albeit 
slowly.  
Attrition in the first seven months of FY 2024 
totaled 21,503 employees, compared to 25,966 
employees during the same period one year ago 
(see Figure 2) and 33,429 employees in FY 2022. 
During fiscal years 2016 through 2019, 
separations from payroll averaged 19,230 
employees during the same seven-month period.  
While the City’s overall attrition rates have 
improved substantially since FY 2022, some 
agencies continue to experience employee 
attrition that greatly exceeds their pre-pandemic 
average. Figure 3 shows the 10 agencies 
currently experiencing the highest percent 
increase in attrition when the year-to-date attrition 
at these agencies is compared to their pre-
pandemic average. For example, the Department 
of Probation experienced, on average, 67 
separations from payroll from July through 
January of each year prior to the pandemic.

[{"content": ""You are a Management Analyst at the City of Greenfield, where the five departments under review total 596 authorized positions (542 filled): Parks & Recreation, Sanitation, Transportation, Health Services, and Fire Department. The City Council will vote on a departmental restructuring proposal, and you must prepare the decision package.

Proposal A (\"Consolidate\") would merge Health Services and Parks & Recreation into \"Community Wellness\" and merge Transportation and Sanitation into \"Public Works,\" with Fire remaining standalone — premised on shared fleet, field crews, and geographic route overlap. Proposal B (\"Targeted Fix\") would retain all five departments but impose cross-training pools, shared overtime budgets for departments exceeding 10% OT-to-regular-hours, and centralized hiring for divisions with vacancy rates above 12%.

Produce three deliverables using the provided data and any relevant NYC municipal benchmarks sourced separately — including the Mayor's Management Report performance indicators and the NYS Comptroller's analysis of post-pandemic city workforce trends.

{"command": "python3 << 'EOF'
import pandas as pd
pd.set_option("display.width", 250); pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None)

sr = pd.read_csv("task_folder/Greenfield_311_Service_Requests_FY2024.csv")
sr["Date_Created"]=pd.to_datetime(sr.Date_Created); sr["Date_Closed"]=pd.to_datetime(sr.Date_Closed)

print("=== counts by dept ==="); print(sr.Department.value_counts())
print("\n=== status by dept ==="); print(pd.crosstab(sr.Department, sr.Status))
print("\n=== resolution days by dept (closed only) ===")
cl = sr[sr.Status=="Closed"]
print(cl.groupby("Department").Resolution_Days.agg(["count","mean","median","max"]).round(2))
print("\n=== satisfaction by dept ===")
print(sr.groupby("Department").Satisfaction_Rating.agg(["count","mean","median"]))
print("\n=== open/in-progress age (days since created to 2024-06-30) ===")
op = sr[sr.Status!="Closed"].copy()
op["age_days"] = (pd.Timestamp("2024-06-30")-op.Date_Created).dt.days
print(op.groupby("Department").age_days.agg(["count","mean","median","max"]).round(1))
print("\n=== resolution days by dept x priority ===")
print(cl.pivot_table(index="Department", columns="Priority", values="Resolution_Days", aggfunc="mean").round(1))
print("\n=== categories by dept (top) ===")
for d in sr.Department.unique():
    print(d, dict(sr[sr.Department==d].Category.value_counts().head(6)))
print("\n=== satisfaction vs resolution days corr ===")
print(sr[["Resolution_Days","Satisfaction_Rating"]].corr().round(3))
print("\n=== by borough ===")
print(pd.crosstab(sr.Borough, sr.Department))
EOF", "description": "Analyze 311 requests by department and status"}

The City Council will vote on a departmental restructuring proposal, and you must prepare the decision package.
2: 
3: Proposal A ("Consolidate") would merge Health Services and Parks & Recreation into "Community Wellness" and merge Transportation and Sanitation into "Public Works," with Fire remaining standalone — premised on shared fleet, field crews, and geographic route overlap. Proposal B ("Targeted Fix") would retain all five departments but impose cross-training pools, shared overtime budgets for departments exceeding 10% OT-to-regular-hours, and centralized hiring for divisions with vacancy rates above 12%.
4: 
5: Produce three deliverables using the provided data and any relevant NYC municipal benchmarks sourced separately — including the Mayor's Management Report performance indicators and the NYS Comptroller's analysis of post-pandemic city workforce trends.
6: 
7: The first deliverable is a Decision Briefing Memo (.docx, 6–10 pages) that opens with a situation overview cross-referencing staffing health against citizen service outcomes, followed by a comparative benchmark analysis contextualizing Greenfield's performance relative to NYC analogs. The memo must evaluate each proposal's impact on process bottlenecks, overtime cost structure, service delivery risk for underperforming SLAs, and workforce feasibility — then close with a clear recommendation (one proposal or a defined hybrid) backed by quantitative arguments and explicit assumptions.
8: 
9: The second deliverable is a Cost-Benefit Analysis Workbook (.xlsx) with four tabs. "Baseline Metrics" should present a department scorecard covering vacancy rate, OT percentage, average 311 resolution days, worst on-time process percentage, and Greenfield-vs-NYC per-employee budget ratio, with red conditional formatting applied where vacancy exceeds 12%, OT exceeds 10%, or on-time falls below 65%. "Proposal A Model" should project merged-department headcount, combined OT costs, and cycle times with documented assumptions for overlapping divisions and shared-fleet savings. "Proposal B Model" should show cross-training pool sizes, OT budget caps, and centralized hiring targets, identifying which divisions currently trigger each intervention. "Comparison Summary" should compare both proposals side-by-side on five dimensions — annual cost savings, FTE reallocation count, projected SLA improvement, implementation complexity (1–5), and risk rating (1–5) — with a net recommendation score.
10: 
11: The third deliverable is a Council Presentation (.pptx, 8–12 slides) summarizing current operational health, the trade-offs between proposals in table or chart form, NYC benchmark context, and a recommendation with next steps.
12: 
13: All quantitative claims must be internally consistent across all three deliverables and traceable to source data.
14: 
15: The NYC benchmark analysis should incorporate the externally sourced Mayor's Management Report (MMR) agency performance indicators (NYC Open Data dataset rbed-zzin) for DPR, DSNY, DOT, DOHMH, and FDNY — focusing on service-level agreement metrics and response time targets — and the NYS Comptroller's "2024 Update on New York City Staffing Trends" (Report 2-2025), covering post-pandemic vacancy rates, agency-level attrition, and overtime spending growth.
16:

18: - Greenfield_311_Service_Requests_FY2024.csv

20: - NYC_Expense_Budget_Selected.csv

{"command": "python3 << 'EOF'
import pandas as pd
pd.set_option("display.width", 250); pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None)
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.2f}")

xl = pd.ExcelFile("task_folder/Greenfield_Dept_Staffing_Overtime_FY2024.xlsx")
ss = xl.parse("Staffing_Summary"); mo = xl.parse("Monthly_Overtime"); pm = xl.parse("Process_Metrics")

print("=== STAFFING SUMMARY (all 20 rows) ===")
print(ss.to_string())
print("\n=== staffing dept totals ===")
g = ss.groupby("Department").agg(auth=("Authorized_Positions","sum"), filled=("Filled_Positions","sum"),
    avg_sal=("Avg_Annual_Salary","mean"), vac_min=("Vacancy_Rate_Pct","min"), vac_max=("Vacancy_Rate_Pct","max"))
g["vac_rate"] = (1 - g.filled/g.auth)*100
print(g.to_string())
print("TOTAL auth:", ss.Authorized_Positions.sum(), "filled:", ss.Filled_Positions.sum())

print("\n=== MONTHLY OT: dept-level aggregates over 12 months ===")
gm = mo.groupby("Department").agg(reg=("Regular_Hours","sum"), ot=("Overtime_Hours","sum"),
    ot_cost=("Overtime_Cost_USD","sum"), n=("Month","count"))
gm["ot_pct"] = gm.ot/gm.reg*100
print(gm.to_string())
print("months per dept:", mo.groupby("Department")["Month"].nunique().to_dict())

print("\n=== PROCESS METRICS (all 26 rows) ===")
print(pm.to_string())
EOF", "description": "Examine Greenfield staffing, overtime, process sheets"}

6: # Building and verifying deliverables

14: ## 3. Excel mechanics (openpyxl)
15: - Write computed values, not formulas: nothing recalculates them, so any `data_only` reader sees None where a number should be.

17: - Put the weighting rationale / assumptions block on the tab that uses it, not only in chat.
18: - Scratch and intermediate files go to /tmp — or a workspace dotfolder such as `.scratch/` when /tmp is blocked — never into the deliverables folder.

20: ## 4. Word mechanics (python-docx)

The City Council will vote on a departmental restructuring proposal, and you must prepare the decision package.
2: 
3: Proposal A ("Consolidate") would merge Health Services and Parks & Recreation into "Community Wellness" and merge Transportation and Sanitation into "Public Works," with Fire remaining standalone — premised on shared fleet, field crews, and geographic route overlap. Proposal B ("Targeted Fix") would retain all five departments but impose cross-training pools, shared overtime budgets for departments exceeding 10% OT-to-regular-hours, and centralized hiring for divisions with vacancy rates above 12%.
4: 
5: Produce three deliverables using the provided data and any relevant NYC municipal benchmarks sourced separately — including the Mayor's Management Report performance indicators and the NYS Comptroller's analysis of post-pandemic city workforce trends.
6: 
7: The first deliverable is a Decision Briefing Memo (.docx, 6–10 pages) that opens with a situation overview cross-referencing staffing health against citizen service outcomes, followed by a comparative benchmark analysis contextualizing Greenfield's performance relative to NYC analogs. The memo must evaluate each proposal's impact on process bottlenecks, overtime cost structure, service delivery risk for underperforming SLAs, and workforce feasibility — then close with a clear recommendation (one proposal or a defined hybrid) backed by quantitative arguments and explicit assumptions.
8: 
9: The second deliverable is a Cost-Benefit Analysis Workbook (.xlsx) with four tabs. "Baseline Metrics" should present a department scorecard covering vacancy rate, OT percentage, average 311 resolution days, worst on-time process percentage, and Greenfield-vs-NYC per-employee budget ratio, with red conditional formatting applied where vacancy exceeds 12%, OT exceeds 10%, or on-time falls below 65%. "Proposal A Model" should project merged-department headcount, combined OT costs, and cycle times with documented assumptions for overlapping divisions and shared-fleet savings. "Proposal B Model" should show cross-training pool sizes, OT budget caps, and centralized hiring targets, identifying which divisions currently trigger each intervention. "Comparison Summary" should compare both proposals side-by-side on five dimensions — annual cost savings, FTE reallocation count, projected SLA improvement, implementation complexity (1–5), and risk rating (1–5) — with a net recommendation score.
10: 
11: The third deliverable is a Council Presentation (.pptx, 8–12 slides) summarizing current operational health, the trade-offs between proposals in table or chart form, NYC benchmark context, and a recommendation with next steps.
12: 
13: All quantitative claims must be internally consistent across all three deliverables and traceable to source data.
14: 
15: The NYC benchmark analysis should incorporate the externally sourced Mayor's Management Report (MMR) agency performance indicators (NYC Open Data dataset rbed-zzin) for DPR, DSNY, DOT, DOHMH, and FDNY — focusing on service-level agreement metrics and response time targets — and the NYS Comptroller's "2024 Update on New York City Staffing Trends" (Report 2-2025), covering post-pandemic vacancy rates, agency-level attrition, and overtime spending growth.

1: You are a Management Analyst at the City of Greenfield, where the five departments under review total 596 authorized positions (542 filled): Parks & Recreation, Sanitation, Transportation, Health Services, and Fire Department. The City Council will vote on a departmental restructuring proposal, and you must prepare the decision package.
2: 
3: Proposal A ("Consolidate") would merge Health Services and Parks & Recreation into "Community Wellness" and merge Transportation and Sanitation into "Public Works," with Fire remaining standalone — premised on shared fleet, field crews, and geographic route overlap. Proposal B ("Targeted Fix") would retain all five departments but impose cross-training pools, shared overtime budgets for departments exceeding 10% OT-to-regular-hours, and centralized hiring for divisions with vacancy rates above 12%.
4: 
5: Produce three deliverables using the provided data and any relevant NYC municipal benchmarks sourced separately — including the Mayor's Management Report performance indicators and the NYS Comptroller's analysis of post-pandemic city workforce trends.
6: 
7: The first deliverable is a Decision Briefing Memo (.docx, 6–10 pages) that opens with a situation overview cross-referencing staffing health against citizen service outcomes, followed by a comparative benchmark analysis contextualizing Greenfield's performance relative to NYC analogs. The memo must evaluate each proposal's impact on process bottlenecks, overtime cost structure, service delivery risk for underperforming SLAs, and workforce feasibility — then close with a clear recommendation (one proposal or a defined hybrid) backed by quantitative arguments and explicit assumptions.
8: 
9: The second deliverable is a Cost-Benefit Analysis Workbook (.xlsx) with four tabs. "Baseline Metrics" should present a department scorecard covering vacancy rate, OT percentage, average 311 resolution days, worst on-time process percentage, and Greenfield-vs-NYC per-employee budget ratio, with red conditional formatting applied where vacancy exceeds 12%, OT exceeds 10%, or on-time falls below 65%. "Proposal A Model" should project merged-department headcount, combined OT costs, and cycle times with documented assumptions for overlapping divisions and shared-fleet savings. "Proposal B Model" should show cross-training pool sizes, OT budget caps, and centralized hiring targets, identifying which divisions currently trigger each intervention. "Comparison Summary" should compare both proposals side-by-side on five dimensions — annual cost savings, FTE reallocation count, projected SLA improvement, implementation complexity (1–5), and risk rating (1–5) — with a net recommendation score.
10: 
11: The third deliverable is a Council Presentation (.pptx, 8–12 slides) summarizing current operational health, the trade-offs between proposals in table or chart form, NYC benchmark context, and a recommendation with next steps.
12: 
13: All quantitative claims must be internally consistent across all three deliverables and traceable to source data.
14: 
15: The NYC benchmark analysis should incorporate the externally sourced Mayor's Management Report (MMR) agency performance indicators (NYC Open Data dataset rbed-zzin) for DPR, DSNY, DOT, DOHMH, and FDNY — focusing on service-level agreement metrics and response time targets — and the NYS Comptroller's "2024 Update on New York City Staffing Trends" (Report 2-2025), covering post-pandemic vacancy rates, agency-level attrition, and overtime spending growth.
16: 
17: Local Reference Files:
18: - Greenfield_311_Service_Requests_FY2024.csv
19: - Greenfield_Dept_Staffing_Overtime_FY2024.xlsx
20: - NYC_Expense_Budget_Selected.csv

(End of file - total 20 lines)
</content>

1: ---
2: name: deliverables
3: description: Build and verify the requested file artifacts (xlsx workbooks, docx reports, csv outputs) for a client deliverable task
4: ---
5: 
6: # Building and verifying deliverables
7: 
8: ## 1. Manifest first
9: List every requested artifact with its exact output path, required tabs/sections, columns/fields, and limits (page caps, naming). Confirm each item maps to a line of the task text before building.
10: 
11: ## 2. Skeleton every artifact immediately
12: Create each file with its full structure (tab names, section headings, column headers) plus any values already computed. A complete-but-rough file on disk beats a perfect one that never gets written; improve in place afterwards.
13: 
14: ## 3. Excel mechanics (openpyxl)
15: - Write computed values, not formulas: nothing recalculates them, so any `data_only` reader sees None where a number should be.
16: - Bold headers and frozen top row on data tabs; explicit number formats for currency, percent, and rate columns.
17: - Put the weighting rationale / assumptions block on the tab that uses it, not only in chat.
18: - Scratch and intermediate files go to /tmp — or a workspace dotfolder such as `.scratch/` when /tmp is blocked — never into the deliverables folder.
19: 
20: ## 4. Word mechanics (python-docx)
21: - Use real heading styles for sections; use tables for matrices (go/no-go grids, scoring tables) rather than prose.
22: - Respect page limits; estimate length from word count before finalizing.
23: 
24: ## 5. Verify before closing
25: Run `python3 scripts/verify_artifacts.py <produced files>`: it reopens each file with an independent reader and flags empty sheets, formula-only cells, header-less tabs, and unreadable files. Fix what it flags and re-run. Then walk the manifest item by item against the task text.

(End of file - total 25 lines)
</content>

The City Council will vote on a departmental restructuring proposal, and you must prepare the decision package.

Proposal A (\"Consolidate\") would merge Health Services and Parks & Recreation into \"Community Wellness\" and merge Transportation and Sanitation into \"Public Works,\" with Fire remaining standalone — premised on shared fleet, field crews, and geographic route overlap. Proposal B (\"Targeted Fix\") would retain all five departments but impose cross-training pools, shared overtime budgets for departments exceeding 10% OT-to-regular-hours, and centralized hiring for divisions with vacancy rates above 12%.

Produce three deliverables using the provided data and any relevant NYC municipal benchmarks sourced separately — including the Mayor's Management Report performance indicators and the NYS Comptroller's analysis of post-pandemic city workforce trends.

The first deliverable is a Decision Briefing Memo (.docx, 6–10 pages) that opens with a situation overview cross-referencing staffing health against citizen service outcomes, followed by a comparative benchmark analysis contextualizing Greenfield's performance relative to NYC analogs. The memo must evaluate each proposal's impact on process bottlenecks, overtime cost structure, service delivery risk for underperforming SLAs, and workforce feasibility — then close with a clear recommendation (one proposal or a defined hybrid) backed by quantitative arguments and explicit assumptions.

The second deliverable is a Cost-Benefit Analysis Workbook (.xlsx) with four tabs. \"Baseline Metrics\" should present a department scorecard covering vacancy rate, OT percentage, average 311 resolution days, worst on-time process percentage, and Greenfield-vs-NYC per-employee budget ratio, with red conditional formatting applied where vacancy exceeds 12%, OT exceeds 10%, or on-time falls below 65%. \"Proposal A Model\" should project merged-department headcount, combined OT costs, and cycle times with documented assumptions for overlapping divisions and shared-fleet savings. \"Proposal B Model\" should show cross-training pool sizes, OT budget caps, and centralized hiring targets, identifying which divisions currently trigger each intervention. \"Comparison Summary\" should compare both proposals side-by-side on five dimensions — annual cost savings, FTE reallocation count, projected SLA improvement, implementation complexity (1–5), and risk rating (1–5) — with a net recommendation score.

The third deliverable is a Council Presentation (.pptx, 8–12 slides) summarizing current operational health, the trade-offs between proposals in table or chart form, NYC benchmark context, and a recommendation with next steps.

All quantitative claims must be internally consistent across all three deliverables and traceable to source data.
